Cape York Peninsula is the long finger of land at the far north of Australia, in Queensland, pointing toward New Guinea across the Torres Strait. It is mostly savanna woodland and rainforest, and still one of the least settled parts of the country.

It was home to dozens of Aboriginal peoples, among them the Wik and the Thaayorre on the west coast, the Wuthathi in the north east and the Guugu Yimidhirr around today's Cooktown.

The peninsula saw the first European landing in Australia on record: in 1606 the Dutch ship Duyfken sailed down its west coast (first recorded landing). In 1770 James Cook repaired his ship at the Endeavour River, where his crew met the Guugu Yimidhirr and took the word "kangaroo" from their language.

The Palmer River gold rush of the 1870s brought thousands of miners, followed by cattle stations, missions and police, and much violence. In 1996 the Wik people won a High Court case, Wik Peoples v Queensland, which found that native title could survive on pastoral leases.
